label: Yesha'yahu (Isaiah) — 1QIsa-a — Part 4 — Chapters 42–54
summary_plain: YHWH presents his servant: Behold my servant whom I uphold, my chosen in whom my soul delights — I have put my spirit upon him, he will bring forth justice to the nations. He will not cry aloud or lift up his voice. A bruised reed he will not break. YHWH calls the servant from the womb. The servant gives his back to those who strike him, his cheeks to those who pull out the beard. He is despised and rejected, a man of sorrows acquainted with grief. He was wounded for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities. By his stripes we are healed. He was cut off from the land of the living. YHWH's will was to crush him. He makes himself an offering for guilt.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) and the Orit Ge'ez. The four servant songs (42:1-4, 49:1-6, 50:4-9, 52:13-53:12) are the most contested passages in the entire covenant literature. The DSS read the servant as a mortal figure — either collective Yisra'EL or an individual human prophet. 1QIsa-a column 44, line 14 reads 'he will see light' after the servant's suffering — a reading absent from the Masoretic but confirmed by the Septuagint. The Qumran community never identifies the servant as divine. The Roman Church's reading of these passages as predictions of a divine incarnation is absent from every pre-Roman Hebrew source.

key_terms.definition: Four poems in Yesha'yahu 42, 49, 50, and 52-53 describing YHWH's Servant: chosen, spirit-endowed, called to bring justice to the nations, and ultimately bearing the community's suffering.
YHWH declares: 'Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth justice to the nations.'
YHWH calls Cyrus king of Persia 'my anointed' (mashiakh) in Yesha'yahu 44:28 and 45:1; Cyrus will authorize the rebuilding of the Temple without knowing YHWH.
Second Servant Song: YHWH says the Servant is 'too small a thing' to restore only Yisra'el; he is given as 'a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.'
The Fourth Servant Song describes one who is disfigured, despised, and bears the community's transgressions; this ancient Hebrew text is the source the NT borrowed its suffering-figure language from.

The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) has significant orthographic and textual differences from the Masoretic Text in chapter 53, confirming that the Masoretic Text is a later editorial layer, not the original.
Yesha'yahu 53:5 — 'he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace.' Ancient Hebrew source text; the NT borrowed from it.
Deutero-Yesha'yahu repeatedly frames the return from Babylon as a New Exodus: YHWH will make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert, surpassing even the original Exodus from Mitzrayim.
YHWH's act of bringing Yisra'el out of Babylon is framed as a redemption (ge'ulah); YHWH is the go'el — the kinsman-redeemer — who buys back his people from bondage.
Yesha'yahu 54:17 — 'no weapon that is fashioned against you shall succeed, and you shall refute every tongue that rises against you in judgment. This is the heritage of the servants of YHWH.'

faq.question: Who is the Servant in the Servant Songs of Yesha'yahu?
faq.answer: The Servant is identified as Yisra'el in some passages (Yesha'yahu 49:3) and as an individual figure within Yisra'el in others. The four songs trace a progression: chosen and spirit-endowed (42), called from the womb (49), opened to suffering without turning back (50), and finally the community's suffering borne by one on behalf of many (52-53). The NT later borrowed the suffering-servant imagery, but the ancient texts are the source.

faq.question: Why does YHWH call Cyrus 'anointed' (mashiakh)?
faq.answer: In Yesha'yahu 44:28 and 45:1, YHWH calls Cyrus of Persia 'my shepherd' and 'my anointed' because YHWH uses him as the instrument to authorize the rebuilding of Yerushalayim and the Temple. Cyrus will do this without knowing YHWH — the anointing is functional, not covenantal. This is the only place in the Hebrew corpus where a foreign king receives this title.

faq.question: What are the DSS textual variants in Yesha'yahu 53?
faq.answer: The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) from Qumran has differences from the Masoretic Text in chapter 53. One significant variant: where the MT reads 'he disfigured him' (53:14), 1QIsa-a reads 'I disfigured him.' These variants confirm the MT is a later editorial layer, not the original text. The pre-Masoretic text is the primary witness.

faq.question: What is the New Exodus theme in Yesha'yahu 43-55?
faq.answer: YHWH announces: 'Remember not the former things; behold, I am doing a new thing' (43:18-19). The return from Babylon will surpass the Exodus from Mitzrayim: YHWH will make rivers in the desert, roads through the wilderness, and lead the exiles back as a second great act of redemption. The covenant community's story is framed as an ongoing liberation narrative.

faq.question: What does the Fourth Servant Song teach about suffering and community?
faq.answer: Yesha'yahu 52:13-53:12 describes a figure whose suffering is at first incomprehensible (53:1-3) but then revealed as vicarious: 'he bore our griefs and carried our sorrows' (53:4); 'he was pierced for our transgressions' (53:5). The community confesses it went astray while he bore the burden. This is communal covenant theology: one bearing for many, not personal punishment.

faq.question: What is the significance of 'light to the nations' in Yesha'yahu 49:6?
faq.answer: The Second Servant Song declares that restoring Yisra'el alone would be 'too small a thing' for the Servant; YHWH's salvation through him must reach the ends of the earth. This frames Yisra'el's covenant role as global — not exclusive to one people but as a demonstration and vehicle of YHWH's universal redemption.

faq.question: What does Yesha'yahu 44:9-20 say about idol-makers?
faq.answer: The extended idol-making polemic (44:9-20) describes a craftsman who plants a cedar, nourishes it with rain, then cuts it down: half goes into the fire for warmth and baking bread; from the remaining half he carves a god, falls down before it and prays 'Save me, for you are my god.' The polemic's conclusion: 'He feeds on ashes; a deluded heart has led him astray' (44:20).

faq.question: What promise does Yesha'yahu 54:10 make about YHWH's covenant of peace?
faq.answer: Yesha'yahu 54:10 — 'For the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but my steadfast love shall not depart from you, and my covenant of peace shall not be removed, says YHWH who has compassion on you.' This covenant of peace (brit shalom) is unconditional; it is more stable than the creation itself.

faq.question: Why is Yesha'yahu 53:7's 'lamb led to slaughter' significant?
faq.answer: The lamb image in Yesha'yahu 53:7 describes the Servant's silence in the face of oppression. It is an ancient Hebrew image of complete submission to suffering without resistance or complaint. This text — not anything from the NT — is the original; all later lamb-of-sacrifice imagery borrowed from this ancient source.

faq.question: What does 'no weapon formed against you shall succeed' mean in context?
faq.answer: Yesha'yahu 54:17 concludes the great consolation section with an assurance to the restored covenant community: every weapon crafted against them will fail, and every legal accusation will be refuted. 'This is the heritage of the servants of YHWH' — the collective promise belongs to the whole community, not a single individual.

faq.question: Who does Yesha'yahu 42:4 say the coastlands will wait for?
faq.answer: The First Servant Song ends: 'He will not grow faint or be discouraged till he has established justice in the earth; and the coastlands wait for his Torah.' The coastal nations and distant peoples will receive YHWH's teaching (Torah) through the Servant's work of bringing justice to the earth.
